turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: If you truly wish to defend Wickham, I must warn you that his actions have been grossly misrepresented in the past, and I will not be swayed by empty apologies.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: I am shocked, Miss Elizabeth, that you would impugn my judgment in such a manner, and defend Wickham's ill-repute.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: You may be shocked, Mr. Darcy, but I am not surprised. Your defense of Wickham's dishonorable behavior only serves to confirm the low opinion I have of you.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: I must confess, Miss Elizabeth, that your continued resistance to my affections only serves to strengthen my resolve, and I shall not be deterred by your shallow and unfounded objections.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: I must ask, Mr. Darcy, why you continue to pursue me when you are so clearly unaware of the harm your actions have caused, and when I have made it abundantly clear that I have no interest in you.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: I must remind you, Miss Elizabeth, that my actions have been guided by a sense of duty and loyalty to my family, and I will not be judged by your limited understanding of the world.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: Your sense of duty and loyalty are admirable, Mr. Darcy, but they do not excuse your behavior towards me, nor do they justify your attempts to buy my affections with your wealth and title.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: I must insist, Miss Elizabeth, that you are not in a position to lecture me on propriety, given your own family's checkered history and your own propensity for misjudging those around you.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: Your attempt to shift the blame onto my family is a cheap tactic, Mr. Darcy, and it will not sway me from my conviction that you are not worthy of my regard.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: I must confess, Miss Elizabeth, that I find your continued obstinacy to be a source of great frustration, and I begin to wonder if your feelings towards me are not, in fact, a reflection of your own personal biases and prejudices.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: Your arrogance is astounding, Mr. Darcy. You seem to believe that your wealth and status grant you a license to behave however you please, without regard for the consequences of your actions or the feelings of those around you.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: I implore you, Miss Elizabeth, to consider the sincerity of my affections, and not let your own prejudices cloud your judgment.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: I am not so foolish as to believe that your words are sincere, Mr. Darcy, for you have shown me time and time again that your actions do not match your words.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: I must admit, Miss Elizabeth, that I find your refusal to consider my proposal to be most disappointing, and I begin to wonder if you are capable of appreciating the depth of my feelings.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: Your feelings are of no consequence to me, Mr. Darcy, and I will not be swayed by your attempts to manipulate me with empty words.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: I must confess, Miss Elizabeth, that I find your obstinacy to be quite... distressing, and I begin to wonder if you are truly worthy of the affections I have professed.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: I am not distressed, Mr. Darcy, but rather relieved to be free from the weight of your condescending affection.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: You wound me, Miss Elizabeth, with your cruel words, and I must take umbrage with your impertinence.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: Your pride is no doubt wounded, Mr. Darcy, but I assure you, it is not I who have caused you harm, but rather your own arrogance and condescending behavior.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: I am astonished, Miss Elizabeth, that you would so callously disregard the sincerity of my emotions, and instead choose to focus on my character, as if it were a matter for public debate.

opening.speaker: Mr. Darcy
opening.text: In vain have I struggled. It will not do. My feelings will not be repressed. You must allow me to tell you how ardently I admire and love you.

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: In such cases as this, it is, I believe, the established mode to express a sense of obligation for the sentiments avowed, however unequally they may be returned. It is natural that obligation should be felt, and if I could feel gratitude, I would now thank you. But I cannot--I have never desired your good opinion, and you have certainly bestowed it most unwillingly. I am sorry to have occasioned pain to anyone. It has been most unconsciously done, however, and I hope will be of short duration. The feelings which you tell me have long prevented the acknowledgment of your regard can have little difficulty in overcoming it after this explanation.

opening.speaker: Mr. Darcy
opening.text: And this is all the reply which I am to have the honour of expecting! I might, perhaps, wish to be informed why, with so little endeavour at civility, I am thus rejected. But it is of small importance.

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: I might as well inquire, why, with so evident a design of offending and insulting me, you chose to tell me that you liked me against your will, against your reason, and even against your character? Was not this some excuse for incivility, if I was uncivil? But I have other provocations. You know I have. Had not my own feelings decided against you, had they been indifferent, or had they even been favourable, do you think that any consideration would tempt me to accept the man who has been the means of ruining, perhaps for ever, the happiness of a most beloved sister?

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: I have every reason in the world to think ill of you. No motive can excuse the unjust and ungenerous part you acted there. You dare not, you cannot deny that you have been the principal, if not the only means of dividing them from each other, of exposing one to the censure of the world for caprice and instability, the other to its derision for disappointed hopes, and involving them both in misery of the acutest kind.

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: Can you deny that you have done it?

opening.speaker: Mr. Darcy
opening.text: I have no wish of denying that I did everything in my power to separate my friend from your sister, or that I rejoice in my success. Towards him I have been kinder than towards myself.

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: But it is not merely this affair, on which my dislike is founded. Long before it had taken place, my opinion of you was decided. Your character was unfolded in the recital which I received many months ago from Mr. Wickham. On this subject, what can you have to say? In what imaginary act of friendship can you here defend yourself? or under what misrepresentation can you here impose upon others?

opening.speaker: Mr. Darcy
opening.text: You take an eager interest in that gentleman’s concerns.

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: Who that knows what his misfortunes have been can help feeling an interest in him?

opening.speaker: Mr. Darcy
opening.text: yes, his misfortunes have been great indeed.
